the superposition of several eddy current signals can be used to size defects much more deeply than the depth of eddy current penetration, and that genetic algorithm can be used to evaluate defect profiles from measured eddy current signals.
superposing eddy current distributions can enlarge the depth of penetration and that genetic algorithms are effective for inverse problems of eddy current nondestructive testing.
a probe with a large exciter and a detector, superposing eddy current distributions, enables one to size deeper defects from eddy current signal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a probe that enables one to size deeper defects and a method to solve inverse problems of the probe.
the use of eddy currents to detect, characterize, and monitor defects in conductive structures.
the development of a new type of probe and a method to solve the inverse problems of evaluating the profile of defects much deeper than that of the depth of penetration.

eddy current distributions superposed in the depth direction are capable of detecting deeper defects than the depth of eddy current penetration.

the probe is useful for detecting defects deeper than the depth-of-penetration and the inverse problem is solvable even if a defect is much deeper than the penetration depth.
eddy current signals due to deep defects can be used for defect sizing even though they are much deeper than the penetration depth.
